newsitem.title: EGYPT: Islamist circumcision victory rings alarm in Egypt.
newsitem.headline: Islamist circumcision victory rings alarm in Egypt.

text.p: Egyptian human rights activists and intellectuals on Wednesday warned the government that Islamists could pull the rug from under its feet by successfully using the courts to further their ideology.

Islamists celebrated their latest victory on Tuesday when a Cairo court championed their cause against the government by declaring null and void a ministerial ban on the ancient practice of female circumcision.

One activist said policy on Islamists was confused. The government seems to have largely ignored the Islamist's judicial challenge to civil society but has met with brute force that of their more militant brothers in southern Egypt, he said.

Over the past couple of years, Islamists have successfully sued to separate a happily married academic couple on the grounds that the husband's writings had made him an apostate and to ban a film by a leading director which they say broke the taboo on the depiction of prophets.
Islamist clerics have also recommended the banning of dozens of books and branded a philosophy professor an apostate for his work. They have urged the professor be banned from teaching.

Islamist Sheikh Youssef el-Badri, who spearheaded the campaign against the health minister's ban on state hospitals and clinics carrying out female circumcisions -- which activists refer to as genital mutilation for the severe form it often takes -- celebrated Tuesday's ruling as a victory for Islam.

"I will prostrate myself before Allah, thanking him for inspiring the court to take this decision. This is a return to Islam," said Badri, a former MP turned preacher who also led the campaign by Islamist lawyers to divorce university professor Nasr Abu Zeid and his academic wife Ibtihal Younis.
Islamists said Abu Zeid's writings had made him an apostate and that his marriage to the Moslem Younis had become null. The couple now live and teach in the Netherlands.

"There is a real crisis in Egyptian society, it is half-secular half-religious. The government has not decided what it wants to be. Egyptian civil society is stuck between a rock and a hard place, between the government and the Islamists," human rights activist Hisham Mubarak told Reuters.

"There's a contradiction -- the government doesn't have enough power to confront a backward Islamist ideology that's trying to Islamise the judiciary and to curb freedoms but it has enough power to confront violent Islamist groups. It has left civil society and intellectuals as prey in the hands of the Islamists," said Mubarak of the independent Centre for Human Rights Legal Aid.
More than 1,000 people, mostly militants and policemen, have died in political violence in Egypt since militants took up arms against the government in 1992.
Military and state security courts have sent dozens of militants to the gallows for staging violent attacks in their attempt to turn Egypt into a strict Islamic state.
But intellectuals complain that the government has done nothing to stand up to attempts by non-violent Islamists to model Egypt to their vision of an Islamic society.
"It is sad. Islamists are gaining all the time. Judges are playing to the gallery knowing they will gain in popularity by such decisions, which are catastrophic," said Egyptian writer Hussein Amin.
Amin chided the government for shrugging its shoulders at Islamist-backed court victories on the grounds that the judiciary was independent.

"The government should ignore the court's decision and look into the phenomemon of fundamentalists invading the courts and legal circles. We are trying to move into the 21st century and our move is being tied up by reactionary forces. These people are fascists and should be dealt with as such with no eye on niceties or democracy," Amin said.
